candidate.answerReason: The three disjoint nonzero cases contain 10, 12, and 13 indices, contributing 110, 156, and 182. Their sum is 448.

methods.label: Count each nonzero case
methods.explanation:
Most terms are zero, so count the indices giving each nonzero value. The numbers \(11\), \(13\), and \(14\) have no common factor greater than \(1\) in any pair. Thus their pairwise least common multiples are
\[
13\cdot14=182,\qquad
14\cdot11=154,\qquad
11\cdot13=143.
\]
We must also check that the cases do not overlap. An index satisfying two nonzero conditions would be divisible by all three numbers, hence by
\[
11\cdot13\cdot14=2002.
\]
No positive index below \(2002\) has this property, so every nonzero term belongs to exactly one case.

For \(a_n=11\), the indices are \(n=182k\) with \(1\le k\le10\). For \(a_n=13\), they are \(n=154k\) with \(1\le k\le12\). For \(a_n=14\), they are \(n=143k\) with \(1\le k\le13\). These ranges are exhaustive because the next multiple in each case is exactly \(2002\), which is excluded.

Therefore
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{2001}a_n
=11\cdot10+13\cdot12+14\cdot13
=110+156+182
=\boxed{448},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
methods.levelReason: Least common multiples and counting bounded positive integer multipliers suffice; no formal floor-function machinery is needed.
